topic_text: Topic 1.6/1.9/1.10: Percentage-of-completion method with a mid-contract variation changing total contract value and estimated cost
question_html:
Constructions Limited is engaged in the business of constructing Flyovers and Railway over bridges. It obtained a contract from Railway Authorities to construct a railway over bridge for ₹400 crores. The construction of the railway over bridge is expected to be completed in 4 years.

At the outset of the contract, it was estimated that the total costs to be incurred will be ₹370 crores but by the end of year 1, this estimate stands revised to ₹375 crores.

During year 3, the Construction Limited has requested for a variation in the contract which is approved by Railway Authorities and accordingly the total contract value will increase by ₹10 crores and costs will increase by ₹7 crores.

The Constructions Limited decided to measure the stage of completion on the basis of the proportion of contract costs incurred to the total estimated contract costs. Contract costs incurred at the end of each year is: Year 1 ₹98.8 crores; Year 2 ₹202.4 crores; Year 3 ₹310 crores (including unused material of 3 crores); Year 4 ₹382 crores.

You are required to: (1) Calculate stage of completion of contract for each year; (2) Profit to be recognised for each year.
answer_html:
(i) Stage of completion = Costs incurred to date / Total estimated costs

YearCalculationStage of completion
Year 198.8 crore / 375 crore26.35%
Year 2202.4 crore / 375 crore53.97%
Year 3(310 crore − 3 crore) / (375+7) crore80.37%
Year 4382 crore / 382 crore100%

(ii) Profit to be recognized each year:

ParticularsYear 1Year 2Year 3Year 4
Contract Revenue (1)105.40 crore (400 crore × 26.35%)110.48 crore (400 crore × 53.97% − 105.40 crore)113.64 crore (410 crore × 80.37% − 105.40 crore − 110.48 crore)80.48 crore (410 crore × 100% − 105.40 − 110.48 − 113.64 crore)
Contract Cost (2)98.8 crore103.60 crore (202.40 − 98.80 crore)104.60 crore (307 crore − 98.8 crore − 103.60 crore)75 crore (382 crore − 98.8 crore − 103.6 crore − 104.6 crore)
Contract Profit (1)−(2)6.60 crore6.88 crore9.04 crore5.48 crore
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is failing to re-base the stage-of-completion percentage each year against the year's own revised total estimated cost, particularly once a contract variation changes both the total contract value and the total estimated cost part-way through the project.

topic_text: Topic 1.6/1.9/1.10: Percentage of completion method - stage of completion via costs-incurred-to-date/total-estimated-costs, revision of contract price and cost estimates mid-contract (change in estimate), profit recognised as revenue less cost incurred each year
question_html:
Constructions Limited is engaged in the business of constructing Flyovers and Railway over bridges. It obtained a contract from Railway Authorities to construct a railway over bridge for ₹400 crores. The construction of the railway over bridge is expected to be completed in 4 years.

At the outset of the contract, it was estimated that the total costs to be incurred will be ₹370 crores but by the end of year 1, this estimate stands revised to ₹375 crores.

During year 3, the Construction Limited has requested for a variation in the contract which is approved by Railway Authorities and accordingly the total contract value will increase by ₹10 crores and costs will increase by ₹7 crores.

mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: Most examinees showed a lack of knowledge of the provisions of AS 7 Construction Contracts. They were required to calculate the percentage of stage of completion for each of the four years. While many did this correctly, some made errors in Year 1 by not considering the revised estimated expenditure, leading to incorrect percentages. A few examinees calculated the percentage completion for each year instead of the stage of completion and failed to calculate the profit to be recognized each year. Some mistook contract revenue for contract profit, and others incorrectly used cumulative figures to determine annual profit without separately calculating contract revenue and contract cost for each year.

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Percentage of completion method - stage of completion, revenue and profit recognition, updated for a contract-price escalation clause
question_html:
Rose Constructions undertake to construct a bridge for the Government of Uttar Pradesh. The construction commenced during the financial year ending 31.03.2024 and is likely to be completed by the next financial year. The contract is for a fixed price of ₹12 crore with an escalation clause. You are given the following information for the year ended 31.03.2024:

Cost incurred upto 31.03.2024₹4 crore
Cost estimated to complete the contract₹6 crore

Escalation in cost was by 5%. Hence, the contract price is also increased by 5%.

You are required to ascertain the stage of completion and compute the amount of revenue and profit to be recognized for the year as per AS 7.
answer_html:
Cost of construction of bridge incurred upto 31.3.2024₹4.00 crore
Add: Estimated future cost₹6.00 crore
Total estimated cost of construction₹10.00 crore
Contract Price (12 crore × 1.05)₹12.60 crore

Stage of completion: Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (4/10)×100 = 40%.

Revenue and Profit to be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per AS 7:

Proportion of total contract value recognized as revenue = Contract price × percentage of completion = ₹12.60 crore × 40% = ₹5.04 crore.

Profit for the year ended 31st March, 2024 = ₹5.04 crore − ₹4 crore = ₹1.04 crore.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is computing the percentage of completion using the original (pre-escalation) contract price or cost estimates instead of updating both cost incurred/estimated-to-complete and contract price for the 5% escalation before applying AS 7's percentage of completion formula.

topic_text: Topic 3.4: Percentage of completion method - unused stored materials excluded from the cost-incurred-to-date figure used to measure progress
question_html: A construction contractor entered a fixed-price contract of ₹18,000 lacs to construct a bridge within 3 years, with provisions for variations. (₹ in lacs): Year 1/2/3 — Initial revenue agreed 18,000/18,000/18,000; Variation in revenue (+)400/400 (Years 2,3); Contract costs incurred to date 4,186/12,336*/16,200**; Estimated profit for whole contract 1,900/2,000/2,000. *includes ₹200 lacs standard materials stored at site for use in Year 3. **excludes ₹200 lacs standard material brought forward from Year 2. Year 2's variation was approved by the customer. Compute year-wise: revenue recognised, expenses recognised, contract costs to complete, and profit/loss recognised.
answer_html:
Working — degree of completion each year (costs incurred, excluding unused stored materials, ÷ estimated total cost): Year 1: revenue after variations 18,000, less estimated profit 1,900 = estimated total cost 16,100; actual cost incurred 4,186; degree of completion = 4,186/16,100 = 26%. Year 2: revenue 18,400, less profit 2,000 = total cost 16,400; cost incurred (excluding the ₹200 lacs stored materials not yet used) 12,336−200=12,136; degree of completion = 12,136/16,400 = 74%. Year 3: revenue 18,400, total cost 16,400; cost incurred 16,200+200 (bringing forward the previously-excluded stored material, now used) = 16,400; degree of completion 100%.

Profit recognised each year: Year 1: 494 (4,680−4,186). Year 2 cumulative 1,480, current year 986 (1,480−494). Year 3 cumulative 2,000, current year 520 (2,000−1,480).

Contract costs to complete the remaining work: Year 1: 16,100−4,186=11,914. Year 2: 16,400−12,136=4,264 (plus the ₹200 lacs stored materials earmarked for Year 3, held separately). Year 3: Nil (contract complete).

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Percentage of completion computed as cost incurred to date (excluding unused materials, including specific/sub-contract costs, excluding advances) over total estimated contract cost
question_html:

  1. Contract Price - ₹85 lakhs
  2. Materials issued - ₹21 Lakhs out of which Materials costing ₹4 Lakhs is still lying unused at the end of the period.

  4. Specific Contract Costs = ₹5 Lakhs

topic_text: Topic 1.3: Conditions under which one contract document covering multiple assets is treated as separate construction contracts
question_html: AP Ltd., a construction contractor, undertakes the construction of a commercial complex for Kay Ltd. AP Ltd. submitted separate proposals for each of 3 units of the commercial complex. A single agreement is entered into between the two parties. The agreement lays down the value of each of the 3 units, i.e. ₹50 Lakh, ₹60 Lakh and ₹75 Lakh respectively. The agreement also lays down the completion time for each unit. Comment, with reference to AS-7, whether AP Ltd. should treat it as a single contract or three separate contracts.
answer_html:
As per AS 7 'Construction Contracts', when a contract covers a number of assets, the construction of each asset should be treated as a separate construction contract when: (a) separate proposals have been submitted for each asset; (b) each asset has been subject to separate negotiation and the contractor and customer have been able to accept or reject that part of the contract relating to each asset; and (c) the costs and revenues of each asset can be identified.

In the given case, AP Ltd. submitted separate proposals for each of the 3 units, the agreement lays down a separate value and separate completion time for each unit, and the costs/revenues of each unit are identifiable. Therefore, AP Ltd. is required to treat the construction of each unit as a separate construction contract, as the above-mentioned conditions of AS 7 are fulfilled in the given case – notwithstanding that a single agreement document was used.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is concluding it must be a single contract simply because only one agreement document was signed, missing that AS 7 looks at the three specific conditions (separate proposals, separate negotiability, identifiable costs/revenues) rather than the number of physical documents.

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Percentage-of-completion revenue recognition together with immediate recognition of the entire foreseeable loss on a loss-making contract
question_html: On 1st December, 2023, GR Construction Co. Ltd. undertook a contract to construct a building for ₹45 lakhs. On 31st March, 2024, the company found that it had already spent ₹32.50 lakhs on the construction. Additional cost of completion is estimated at ₹15.10 lakhs. What amount should be charged to revenue in the final accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per provisions of AS-7?
answer_html:
₹ in lakhs
Cost of construction incurred till date32.50
Add: Estimated future cost15.10
Total estimated cost of construction47.60

Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (32.50/47.60) × 100 = 68.28%.

Proportion of total contract value recognised as revenue for the year ended 31st March, 2024 per AS 7 (Revised) = Contract price × percentage of completion = ₹45 lakh × 68.28% = ₹30.73 lakhs.

₹ in lakhs
Total cost of construction47.60
Less: Total contract price(45.00)
Total foreseeable loss to be recognized as expense2.60

According to AS 7, when it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognized as an expense immediately (in full, not spread by percentage of completion).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is recognising only the current period's proportionate share of the ₹2.60 lakh foreseeable loss (via the 68.28% completion rate) rather than the entire foreseeable loss immediately, once it becomes probable that total costs will exceed total contract revenue.

topic_text: Topic 3.5: Expected loss on a construction contract recognised immediately in full, regardless of stage of completion
question_html: A company took a construction contract for ₹100 lakhs in January 2024; 80% completed at cost ₹92 lakhs by 31.3.2025; further ₹23 lakhs estimated to complete; expected loss ₹15 lakhs. Can the company recognise the loss in the FY2024-25 financial statements?
answer_html: Yes. Per AS 7 paras 31 and 35, an expected loss on a construction contract must be recognised as an expense immediately, regardless of (i) whether work has commenced; (ii) the stage of completion; or (iii) profits expected on other contracts. The company must recognise the ₹15 lakh loss immediately in the year ended 31.3.2025.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees deferred the loss recognition to future periods or spread it across the remaining completion percentage, missing AS 7's requirement for immediate full recognition.
